title: Butterflies: Caterpillars with Wings!
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck continue their butterfly episode (part two after the caterpillar episode), covering the moth-butterfly distinction, the etymology of "butterfly," butterfly anatomy (eyes, antennae, labial palps, proboscis, legs, wings), emergence from the chrysalis and wing pumping, thermoregulation and basking, migration (monarchs from eastern Canada to Mexico), the 2015 Mexico logging at the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, puddling and mineral/nutrient feeding, mating and spermatophores, egg-laying and host plants, threats from pesticides, habitat loss, roads and collecting, and planting butterfly gardens with native plants (warning against butterfly bush). They close with the Rh blood factor and Sir Cyril Clark anecdote and listener mail about Spotify search associations (Milli Vanilli, Black Sabbath, Barry Manilow).

segments.title: Spring playlist intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the spring playlist episode on butterflies, the second in a two-part series after the caterpillar episode.

segments.title: Picking up after the chrysalis
segments.summary: The hosts recap that the butterfly emerges from a chrysalis with the same mind as the caterpillar but built for reproduction, and reference the previous caterpillar episode.

segments.title: Moths versus butterflies
segments.summary: Butterflies are diurnal and descended from moths that shifted to daytime activity; moths are attracted to the moon for navigation, while butterflies navigate by the sun.

segments.title: Etymology of the word butterfly
segments.summary: The name may come from the pale yellow color resembling butter, or from a folk belief that butterflies were spirits that stole butter and milk, reflected in German and Dutch names.

segments.title: Butterfly eyes and antennae
segments.summary: Butterflies have compound eyes that detect color and movement, and the monarch has about twelve thousand eyes. Antennae sense odors, pheromones, light, and wingbeats, and help with sun-based navigation.

segments.title: Labial palps and proboscis
segments.summary: Labial palps are sensory organs that may detect carbon dioxide; the proboscis is a nectar-sipping tongue that the butterfly assembles from two parts after emerging.

segments.title: Butterfly legs and taste
segments.summary: Butterflies have six legs, with taste organs in their feet that can trigger the proboscis to uncoil on contact with dissolved sugar; one front pair is often shriveled.

segments.title: Butterfly wings and scales
segments.summary: Wing iridescence was covered in an earlier episode. Wings are made of transparent chitin, have veins that are species-specific and used in recognition, and cannot be repaired; damage can be fatal.

segments.title: Emergence, meconium, and wing inflation
segments.summary: Newly emerged butterflies pass meconium, clean their organs, assemble the proboscis, and pump fluid into their wings to expand and dry them before flying. A tangent covers Reebok pump sneakers and Spud Webb.

segments.title: Cliffhanger on cold weather
segments.summary: The hosts set up that newly emerged butterflies find it is not a good day to fly, and promise to explain after a break.

segments.title: Ectotherms, cold weather, and basking
segments.summary: Butterflies are ectotherms whose muscles stop working in cold; optimal internal temperature is about 82 F. Wings are used for defense and warming, and butterflies bask in sun, shiver, and angle wings to warm or cool.

segments.title: Migration and the monarch journey
segments.summary: Around two hundred species migrate; monarchs travel from eastern Canada to northwest Mexico over about eight months, with no butterfly that starts the trip surviving to the end. Butterfly groups are called kaleidoscopes.

segments.title: 2015 logging and population declines
segments.summary: Illegal logging at the Butterfly Biosphere Reserve in Mexico in 2015 cleared acres of forest; monarch numbers fell from about a billion in 1996 to about thirty-five million by 2016, with recent recovery. The reserve is a UNESCO site.

segments.title: Pollination and puddling
segments.summary: Butterflies are less effective pollinators than bees; they puddle to get minerals from soil, and fruit-eating monarchs in a study lived longer and laid more and bigger eggs.

segments.title: Butterfly mating and spermatophores
segments.summary: Males transfer a spermatophore containing sperm and nutrients; females fertilize eggs after laying them, and some males seal the female to prevent later matings. Males may use an off-putting scent.

segments.title: Green veined white and egg laying
segments.summary: The green veined white produces a pheromone chemically similar to lemon oil. Females lay between ten and three hundred eggs over two to four weeks, with humidity and temperature critical to survival.

segments.title: Host plants and butterfly bush
segments.summary: Many butterflies are plant-specific for caterpillar food. Butterfly bush produces nectar but doesn't support caterpillars, so it is considered invasive and a distraction from native plants.

segments.title: Threats: pesticides, caterpillars as pests, roads, urbanization
segments.summary: Pesticides, killing caterpillars as pests, urban development, and roadside traffic all harm butterfly populations; butterflies are indicator species.

segments.title: Butterfly collecting
segments.summary: Collecting butterflies for display harms rare species; the hosts discuss legal protection, antique specimens, and enforcement.

segments.title: Planting butterfly gardens
segments.summary: Advice to identify local butterflies, plant native species, provide water puddles and rocks for basking, and avoid non-native tropical milkweed in the Southeast. Anecdotes about a hornet's nest and the hosts' own gardens and land.

segments.title: Rh blood factor and Cyril Clark
segments.summary: Butterfly mimicry genes reportedly inspired Sir Cyril Clark's discovery of the Rh blood factor, which helped cure hemolytic disease of the newborn.

segments.title: Listener mail: Spotify search associations
segments.summary: A listener notes that searching Owner of a Lonely Heart and Milli Vanilli together on Spotify surfaced both. The hosts test by pairing Black Sabbath's Warpigs with Barry Manilow's Even Now.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to report results of the experiment and give the email address; the episode closes with credits.
